claims.text: Increasing short-range chemical order in an uncharacterized high-entropy alloy enhances electron-phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron-phonon coupling caused by short-range ordering produces a measurable shift in superconducting critical temperature.
The starting material is a homogeneous, single-phase disordered solid solution.
A high-entropy alloy contains at least five elements, each at no less than 5 atomic percent.
Rapid quenching maximizes chemical disorder and minimizes short-range chemical order.
Slow cooling or annealing promotes short-range chemical ordering.
The comparison should be performed at the same constant pressure and under cryogenic conditions near or below 10 K.
The alloy must remain single-phase without precipitation during the comparison.
Short-range chemical order and associated local lattice distortions can be quantified using synchrotron X-ray pair-distribution-function analysis.
Changes in local atomic arrangement modify the phonon spectrum.
Changes in local atomic arrangement modify the strength of electron-phonon interactions.
Local ordering can alter superconducting behavior through changes in the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Slow-cooled samples with greater local order will exhibit a statistically significant shift in critical temperature relative to rapidly quenched samples.
Slow-cooled samples will exhibit an altered electronic density of states relative to rapidly quenched samples.
The magnitude and specific direction of the critical-temperature change are uncertain because disorder and intrinsic material variability may have competing effects.
No statistically significant difference in critical temperature or electronic density of states between ordered and disordered samples would falsify the proposed ordering-based mechanism.
